procedural_history.impugned_order: Conviction and sentence of death passed by the Sessions Judge of Ferozepore on 20th July, 1949, in Criminal Appeal Case No. 325 of 1949, under sections 302 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Punjab (Falshaw and Soni JJ.) upheld the conviction of the appellant under ss. 302 and 307 read with s. 34 of the Indian Penal Code and confirmed the sentence of death in a judgment dated 30th December, 1949.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction, finding that there had been no fair and proper trial.

directions: direct that he be set at liberty forthwith

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court will entertain a criminal appeal only in special and exceptional cases where it is manifest that by a disregard of the forms of legal process or by a violation of the principles of natural justice or otherwise substantial and grave injustice has been done.

facts: The appellant was convicted despite the prosecution's evidence being incomplete on a "most-material part of the prosecution case."
The court also found that the lower courts had improperly handled the appellant's alibi plea, disregarding the standard of proof required.
law: The Supreme Court cited its own precedent from *Pritam Singh v. The State*, which established the rule that the Court will not entertain a criminal appeal except in "special and exceptional cases."

Such cases are defined as those where it is clear ("manifest") that a "substantial and grave injustice has been done" through a disregard of legal process, a violation of natural justice, or other similar failures.
application: The Court applied this established rule to the current case.
It determined that convicting the appellant when the evidence was "wanting on a most-material part of the prosecution case" constituted a "substantial and grave injustice."
The Court also noted that the improper disposal of the alibi plea was another factor indicating that a fair and proper trial had not occurred.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the case fell within the established rule for its intervention. By finding that a grave injustice had occurred due to a conviction based on incomplete evidence and a flawed trial process, the Court confirmed that it will entertain criminal appeals, but only under such special and exceptional circumstances.

issue.issue_text: Whether the standard of proof required in regard to a plea of alibi must be the same as the standard which is applied to the prosecution evidence, and in both cases, it should be a reasonable standard.

facts: The appellant in a criminal case put forward a plea of alibi.
The lower courts heard the plea of alibi and disposed of it, finding that it was not proved by satisfactory evidence.
law: The Supreme Court established the principle that the standard of proof required for a plea of alibi must be the same as the standard applied to the prosecution's evidence.
In both instances, the standard should be a "reasonable standard."
Ordinarily, the Supreme Court will not look beyond the findings of fact made by lower courts.
application: The Supreme Court found that the lower courts had arrived at their decision on the plea of alibi "in disregard of the principle" that the standard of proof must be the same reasonable standard as that applied to the prosecution.
The Court made an exception to its usual practice of not reviewing findings of fact because a fundamental legal principle had been violated in the handling of the alibi plea.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the standard of proof for a plea of alibi must be the same reasonable standard that is applied to the prosecution's evidence. The Court found that the lower courts had erred by failing to apply this principle when they rejected the appellant's alibi.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court will entertain a criminal appeal only in special and exceptional cases where it is manifest that by a disregard of the forms of legal process or by a violation of the principles of natural justice or otherwise substantial and grave injustice has been done.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that their case qualified as a special and exceptional one warranting the Supreme Court's intervention.

They contended that a substantial and grave injustice had been done because they were convicted despite the prosecution's failure to provide evidence on a material part of its case, specifically the lack of expert evidence to prove the injuries could have been caused by the alleged weapon.
respondent_arguments: The respondent would have implicitly argued that the case did not meet the high threshold for a special appeal and that no grave injustice had occurred that would justify the Supreme Court's intervention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the standard of proof required in regard to a plea of alibi must be the same as the standard which is applied to the prosecution evidence, and in both cases, it should be a reasonable standard.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the lower courts had improperly disposed of their plea of alibi.

They contended that the lower courts had disregarded the correct legal principle by applying a different (and likely higher) standard of proof to the alibi defense than the one applied to the prosecution's evidence.
respondent_arguments: The respondent would have implicitly argued that the lower courts correctly evaluated the evidence for the alibi and found it unsatisfactory, and that the correct standard of proof had been applied.

cases.case_name: Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Midnapur Zaminiari Co.
cases.principle: For the principle that a lease, even if covered by cl. (b) of s. 17(1) of the Indian Registration Act, was exempt from registration under cl. (vi) of sub-s. (2) of s. 17.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The standard of proof required in regard to the plea of alibi must be the same as the standard which is applied to the prosecution evidence, and in both cases, it should be a reasonable standard.
obiter: The Supreme Court will not entertain a criminal appeal except in special and exceptional cases where it is manifest that by a disregard of the forms of legal process or by a violation of the principles of natural justice or otherwise substantial and grave injustice has been done.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that a substantial and grave injustice had been done because the appellant was convicted despite the prosecution's failure to prove a most material part of its case. Specifically, the prosecution did not provide expert evidence to establish that the victim's injuries could have been caused by the alleged weapon, which is a fundamental duty of the prosecution in a murder case. This evidentiary gap, combined with the lower courts' improper handling of the appellant's alibi plea, meant that the conviction could not be upheld.
legal_tests_applied: The Supreme Court will not entertain a criminal appeal except in special and exceptional cases where it is manifest that by a disregard of the forms of legal process or by a violation of the principles of natural justice or otherwise substantial and grave injustice has been done.

In a case where death is due to injuries or wounds caused by a lethal weapon, it has always been considered to be the duty of the prosecution to prove by expert evidence that it was likely or at least possible for the injuries to have been caused with the weapon with which and in the manner in which they are alleged to have been caused.

The standard of proof which is required in regard to the plea of alibi must be the same as the standard which is applied to the prosecution evidence and in both cases it should be a reasonable standard.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution failed to meet its burden of proof, as the evidence was 'wanting on a most-material part of the prosecution case.' The Court noted that the evidence adduced 'falls short of proof in regard to a very material part of the prosecution case' because no expert evidence was presented to link the alleged weapon to the injuries.

The lower courts improperly disposed of the appellant's plea of alibi by arriving at their decision 'in disregard of the principle that the standard of proof which is required in regard to that plea must be the same as the standard which is applied to the prosecution evidence.' For example, the Sessions Judge ignored key evidence from the Naib Tehsildar regarding the timing of the appellant's alleged alibi.
policy_considerations: The Court concluded that 'there has been in substance no fair and proper trial in this case,' justifying its intervention to prevent a grave injustice.

The Court declined to order a retrial, reasoning that 'such a course would, in the present case, be unfair and contrary to settled practice, seeing that the appellant has been in a state of suspense over his sentence of death for more than a year.'
